title: Metals and Non-metals
summary: Elements are divided into metals and non-metals on the basis of their physical and chemical properties. This chapter contrasts malleability, ductility, lustre, sonority and conduction, and notes the famous exceptions such as liquid mercury, lustrous iodine and conducting graphite. Chemically, metals react with oxygen to give basic and amphoteric oxides, with water in a vigour that descends down the reactivity series, and with dilute acids to give hydrogen, except with nitric acid, and the special solvent aqua regia is introduced. Electron transfer between a metal and a non-metal forms ionic bonds, giving high-melting, conducting ionic compounds. The chapter then explains how ores are concentrated and reduced by roasting, calcination or electrolysis according to the position of the metal in the reactivity series, including the thermite reaction and electrolytic refining of copper. It ends with corrosion and its prevention by galvanisation and alloying, and the composition and uses of important alloys like brass, bronze, solder and stainless steel.
hotTopics: Physical properties of metals and non-metals with exceptions
Reactions of metals with oxygen and amphoteric oxides
Reactions with water, steam and dilute acids
Aqua regia and the nitric acid exception
The reactivity series and displacement predictions
Formation of ionic bonds and electron transfer
Extraction of low, medium and high reactivity metals
Alloys: brass, bronze, solder, amalgam and stainless steel

sections.heading: Physical Properties: The Metallic Shine and Its Exceptions
sections.para: Metals are usually lustrous, malleable, ductile, sonorous and good conductors of heat and electricity, while non-metals are usually brittle, non-lustrous and poor conductors. But every rule in this chapter comes with exceptions, and CBSE loves these exceptions. All metals except mercury are solid at room temperature, because mercury is a liquid metal used in thermometers. Iodine is a non-metal that has a lustrous shining surface, and graphite, a form of carbon, is the non-metal that conducts electricity, which is why it is used in electrodes. Alkali metals like sodium and potassium are so soft that they can be cut with a knife, and they have low densities, floating on water while reacting violently. Diamond, another allotrope of carbon, is the hardest natural substance though it is non-metallic. Metals have high melting points generally, with gallium and caesium melting on the palm, and metals are used as wires, sheets and utensils because of these very properties.
points: Metals are generally lustrous, malleable (beaten into sheets), ductile (drawn into wires), sonorous and good conductors of heat and electricity.
Non-metals are generally brittle solids or gases, dull, and poor conductors; they are neither malleable nor ductile.
Exception: mercury is the only metal that is liquid at room temperature and is used in thermometers.
Exception: iodine is a lustrous non-metal, and graphite conducts electricity being a non-metal.
Sodium and potassium are soft metals with low density that float on water and react violently, so they are stored under kerosene.
Metals generally have high melting and boiling points, but gallium and caesium melt on the palm of the hand.
Gold and silver are the most ductile and malleable metals, drawn into extremely fine wires and thin foils.

keyTerms.meaning: Property of metals by which they can be beaten into thin sheets.
Property of metals by which they can be drawn into thin wires.
Property of metals of producing a ringing sound when struck.
Term for oxides like Al2O3 that react with both acids and bases.

sections.trick: Exceptions club: Hg is liquid, I2 is lustrous, graphite conducts, Na and K are soft, Ga and Cs melt in the palm. Expect CBSE to test exactly these five.
sections.examPointer: Distinguishing metals from non-metals on physical properties with exceptions is a standard 3-marker; graphite and mercury exceptions are repeated MCQs.

sections.heading: Metals with Oxygen: Basic and Amphoteric Oxides
sections.para: Almost all metals combine with oxygen to form metal oxides: sodium burns to give 4Na + O2 -> 2Na2O, magnesium burns with a dazzling white flame as 2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO, and a red hot iron wool glows in oxygen as 3Fe + 2O2 -> Fe3O4. Metal oxides are basic: they dissolve in water to form alkalis, e.g. Na2O + H2O -> 2NaOH and K2O + H2O -> 2KOH, which turn red litmus blue. But some metal oxides, such as aluminium oxide Al2O3 and zinc oxide ZnO, show both acidic and basic behaviour: they react with acids to form salt and water, Al2O3 + 6HCl -> 2AlCl3 + 3H2O, and also with strong bases, Al2O3 + 2NaOH -> 2NaAlO2 + H2O. Such oxides are called amphoteric oxides. Most metal oxides are insoluble in water, but those that dissolve form alkalis. Non-metals form acidic oxides, e.g. carbon dioxide dissolves in water to give carbonic acid.
points: Metals burn in oxygen forming metal oxides: 4Na + O2 -> 2Na2O and 2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO with dazzling white flame.
Iron wool heated red hot burns in oxygen: 3Fe + 2O2 -> Fe3O4, iron(II,III) oxide.
Metal oxides are basic: Na2O + H2O -> 2NaOH and K2O + H2O -> 2KOH turn red litmus blue.
Amphoteric oxides react with both acids and bases: Al2O3 + 6HCl -> 2AlCl3 + 3H2O and Al2O3 + 2NaOH -> 2NaAlO2 + H2O.
ZnO, like Al2O3, is amphoteric; most other metal oxides are purely basic.
Non-metal oxides are acidic, e.g. CO2 dissolves in water to form carbonic acid, H2CO3.
Sodium and potassium catch fire if left open in air, so they are stored under kerosene.

keyTerms.meaning: Compound of a metal with oxygen, generally basic in nature.
An oxide that reacts with both acids and bases, e.g. Al2O3 and ZnO.
A soluble metal hydroxide formed when an oxide dissolves in water, e.g. NaOH.
Oxide of a non-metal that dissolves in water to form an acid, e.g. CO2.

sections.trick: Amphoteric means both-sided: Al2O3 and ZnO shake hands with acids and bases alike. Metal oxide plus water equals alkali; non-metal oxide plus water equals acid.
sections.examPointer: Identifying amphoteric oxides from a list and writing the two Al2O3 equations is a frequent 2-3 marker; metal oxide litmus behaviour is a regular MCQ.

sections.heading: Metals with Water: Vigour Descends the Series
sections.para: The reaction of metals with water decreases dramatically down the reactivity series. Sodium and potassium react so vigorously with cold water that they catch fire: 2Na + 2H2O -> 2NaOH + H2, and the heat evolved ignites the hydrogen. Calcium reacts less vigorously, sinking while bubbles stick to it: Ca + 2H2O -> Ca(OH)2 + H2. Magnesium does not react with cold water but reacts with hot water to form magnesium hydroxide and hydrogen, Mg + 2H2O -> Mg(OH)2 + H2, and it starts floating as hydrogen bubbles stick to its surface. Metals like aluminium, iron and zinc do not react with cold or hot water but react with steam, the most important example being 3Fe + 4H2O -> Fe3O4 + 4H2. Metals like lead, copper, silver and gold do not react with water at all. This graded behaviour is the practical evidence on which the reactivity series is built.
points: Sodium and potassium react violently with cold water: 2Na + 2H2O -> 2NaOH + H2; the hydrogen catches fire due to the heat released.
Calcium reacts with water less vigorously, sinking while hydrogen bubbles stick to its surface: Ca + 2H2O -> Ca(OH)2 + H2.
Magnesium reacts with hot water forming Mg(OH)2 and H2, and starts floating because of adhering bubbles.
Aluminium, zinc and iron react only with steam; the key equation is 3Fe + 4H2O -> Fe3O4 + 4H2.
Lead, copper, silver and gold do not react with water in any form.
The decreasing vigour from Na to Au against water is direct evidence for arranging metals in the reactivity series.
Sodium and potassium are stored in kerosene to prevent contact with air and moisture.

keyTerms.meaning: List of metals arranged in order of decreasing reactivity, K at top and Au at bottom.
Reaction of moderately reactive metals like iron with steam giving oxide and hydrogen.
Mg(OH)2, product of magnesium with hot water.
Fe3O4, the mixed oxide formed when iron reacts with steam.

sections.trick: Water attack order: Na and K explode, Ca bubbles, Mg needs hot water, Fe needs steam, Cu and Au simply refuse. The colder the water needed, the higher the metal sits in the series.
sections.examPointer: Equations of Na, Ca, Mg and Fe with water plus the storage of sodium in kerosene form a repeated 3-5 mark cluster; the Fe-steam equation is asked almost every year.

sections.heading: Metals with Dilute Acids and the Aqua Regia Exception
sections.para: Metals above hydrogen in the reactivity series displace hydrogen from dilute acids, e.g. Mg + 2HCl -> MgCl2 + H2 and Zn + H2SO4 -> ZnSO4 + H2, the fastest bubbles coming from magnesium. Metals below hydrogen, like copper, silver and gold, give no reaction with dilute acids. Nitric acid is the famous exception: being a strong oxidising agent, it oxidises the hydrogen produced to water and is itself reduced to oxides of nitrogen, so hydrogen gas is generally not evolved when a metal reacts with nitric acid. But magnesium and manganese react with very dilute nitric acid to evolve hydrogen gas. Aqua regia, a fresh mixture of three parts concentrated hydrochloric acid and one part concentrated nitric acid, is one of the strongest corrosive agents and can dissolve even gold and platinum, the least reactive metals; it is highly corrosive and fuming, and its name means royal water.
points: Metals above hydrogen displace it from dilute acids: Mg + 2HCl -> MgCl2 + H2 and Zn + H2SO4 -> ZnSO4 + H2.
Copper, silver and gold do not react with dilute hydrochloric or sulphuric acid.
HNO3 is a strong oxidising agent: it oxidises the hydrogen formed to water and itself reduces to NO2 or NO, so H2 is generally not released.
Exception: Mg and Mn react with very dilute HNO3 to evolve H2 gas.
Aqua regia: freshly prepared 3:1 mixture of concentrated HCl and concentrated HNO3; dissolves gold and platinum.
The order of vigour with dilute acids, Mg > Zn > Fe > Cu, again matches the reactivity series.
Aqua regia is highly corrosive and fuming; it is handled with extreme care in laboratories.

keyTerms.meaning: Freshly prepared 3:1 mixture of conc. HCl and conc. HNO3 that can dissolve gold and platinum.
Nitric acid, which oxidises hydrogen to water instead of releasing it.
Release of H2 gas by metals above hydrogen in the reactivity series when treated with dilute acids.
Mn reacts with very dilute HNO3 to give H2, one of only two such metals with Mg.

sections.trick: Nitric acid is the hydrogen thief: it oxidises H2 to water, except with Mg and Mn in very dilute form. Aqua regia is royal because even the king of metals, gold, dissolves in it.
sections.examPointer: Why H2 is not evolved with HNO3 and the composition of aqua regia are standard 2-markers; both have appeared as assertion-reason and MCQ items.

sections.heading: The Reactivity Series in Action
sections.para: The reactivity series, from most to least reactive, runs approximately K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Pb > H > Cu > Hg > Ag > Au. It is built from observations of displacement reactions: a more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from its salt solution. Aluminium displaces iron: Fe2O3 + 2Al -> Al2O3 + 2Fe, the thermite reaction, and manganese: 3MnO2 + 4Al -> 3Mn + 2Al2O3, so Al is above Fe and Mn. Zinc displaces copper: Zn + CuSO4 -> ZnSO4 + Cu, and copper displaces silver: Cu + 2AgNO3 -> Cu(NO3)2 + 2Ag, so Zn > Cu > Ag. If a metal cannot displace another from its salt, it is less reactive, e.g. Fe cannot displace Zn from ZnSO4. A single look at the position of a metal in this series predicts its behaviour with oxygen, water, acids and the method needed to extract it from its ore.
points: Reactivity series order: K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Pb > H > Cu > Hg > Ag > Au.
More reactive metal displaces less reactive metal from its compound: Zn + CuSO4 -> ZnSO4 + Cu.
Copper displaces silver: Cu + 2AgNO3 -> Cu(NO3)2 + 2Ag, giving Zn > Cu > Ag.
Aluminium displaces iron and manganese: Fe2O3 + 2Al -> Al2O3 + 2Fe and 3MnO2 + 4Al -> 3Mn + 2Al2O3.
If no displacement occurs, the added metal is less reactive, e.g. Fe in ZnSO4 solution shows no change.
Hydrogen occupies a position in the series: metals above H react with dilute acids, metals below H do not.
Position in the series decides the extraction method: electrolysis at the top, chemical reduction in the middle, heating alone at the bottom.

keyTerms.meaning: Order of metals by decreasing chemical reactivity used to predict displacement and extraction.
A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive one from its salt solution.
Aluminium lies above iron, enabling it to reduce Fe2O3.
Hydrogen acts as the dividing line for reaction with dilute acids.

sections.trick: Mnemonic for the series: Please Stop Calling Me A Zebra In Lovely Hotels Closed Monday Since Gold Arrived (P K Na Ca Mg Al Zn Fe Pb H Cu Hg Ag Au). The top bullies always win displacements.
sections.examPointer: Predicting which metal displaces which from the series is a guaranteed question; a 3-marker often gives four metals and four observation sets to arrange.

sections.heading: Ionic Bonding: Metals Give, Non-metals Take
sections.para: Compounds of reactive metals with reactive non-metals are formed by complete transfer of electrons, producing ions that attract each other to form an ionic bond. In sodium chloride, sodium with electronic configuration 2,8,1 loses its single valence electron to become Na+, while chlorine with 2,8,7 gains one electron to become Cl-; the reactions are Na -> Na+ + e- and Cl2 + 2e- -> 2Cl-, and the oppositely charged ions arrange into a crystal of NaCl. In magnesium chloride, magnesium 2,8,2 loses two electrons to form Mg2+, and each of two chlorine atoms takes one electron: Mg -> Mg2+ + 2e- and Cl2 + 2e- -> 2Cl-, giving MgCl2. In magnesium oxide, Mg2+ pairs with O2-. The driving force is the stability of the noble gas configuration: metal atoms empty their outer shell by losing electrons and non-metals complete theirs by gaining, so both reach a full octet.
points: Ionic bond: electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions formed by complete transfer of electrons.
NaCl formation: Na -> Na+ + e- (sodium 2,8,1 becomes 2,8) and Cl2 + 2e- -> 2Cl- (each Cl 2,8,7 becomes 2,8,8).
MgCl2 formation: Mg -> Mg2+ + 2e-; two Cl atoms each accept one electron, giving one Mg2+ for two Cl-, formula MgCl2.
MgO formation: Mg loses two electrons to Mg2+ and oxygen gains two electrons to O2-, a 1:1 ionic solid.
Metals are electropositive: they lose electrons to attain the noble gas configuration; non-metals are electronegative: they gain electrons.
Cation is the positive ion formed by electron loss; anion is the negative ion formed by electron gain.
The number of electrons lost or gained equals the valency, so the formulae follow directly from the charges.

keyTerms.meaning: Bond formed by electrostatic attraction between cations and anions after electron transfer.
Positively charged ion formed when a metal loses electrons, e.g. Na+, Mg2+.
Negatively charged ion formed when a non-metal gains electrons, e.g. Cl-, O2-.
Number of electrons lost, gained or shared by an atom to complete its octet.
Stable filled outer shell arrangement like 2,8 or 2,8,8 achieved after transfer.

sections.trick: Metals donate, non-metals accept: the rich in electrons gives, the poor takes. Na gives 1, Mg gives 2, so NaCl needs one Cl but MgCl2 needs two.
sections.examPointer: Electron transfer schemes for NaCl and MgCl2 with cation and anion formation are classic 3-markers; valency-based formula writing is a regular 1-2 mark item.

sections.heading: Properties of Ionic Compounds
sections.para: Ionic compounds share a distinct set of properties that follow from their structure of strong electrostatic forces between ions. They are generally hard solids with high melting and boiling points, because large amounts of energy are needed to break the strong electrostatic attraction between the oppositely charged ions packed in the crystal lattice. Sodium chloride melts at about 1074 K and magnesium oxide at about 2852 K. They are generally soluble in water but insoluble in organic solvents like kerosene and petrol, because water molecules can surround and stabilise the ions. Most importantly, they conduct electricity in the molten state and in aqueous solution, because the ions become free to move and carry current; in the solid state the ions are held fixed in the lattice, so solids do not conduct. This is why molten NaCl or brine conducts while dry solid NaCl does not, a difference frequently tested in examinations.
points: Ionic compounds are generally hard crystalline solids with high melting and boiling points due to strong interionic forces.
NaCl melts around 1074 K; MgO around 2852 K, showing how much energy the lattice needs.
They are soluble in water because water stabilises the ions, but insoluble in kerosene, petrol and other organic solvents.
In the solid state ions are fixed in the lattice, so ionic solids do not conduct electricity.
In the molten state or in aqueous solution the ions become free to move, so they conduct electricity.
Conducting molten NaCl or brine is the basis of industrial electrolysis for sodium and chlorine production.
Comparison: covalent compounds like naphthalene have low melting points, are insoluble in water and do not conduct.

keyTerms.meaning: Regular three-dimensional arrangement of cations and anions in an ionic solid.
Strong electrostatic force between oppositely charged ions responsible for high melting points.
Free movement of ions in a melted ionic compound allowing electric conduction.
Conduction of electricity by dissolved ions in water.

sections.trick: Ionic checklist HPSC: High melting point, Pink of hardness, Soluble in water, Conducts only when molten or dissolved. Solid ions are locked, melted ions can march.
sections.examPointer: Reasons for high melting point and condition of conductivity of ionic compounds are near-certain 2-3 markers, often contrasted with covalent compounds in tabular questions.

sections.heading: Occurrence and Extraction: Three Zones of the Series
sections.para: Metals occur in nature either in the free native state, like gold, silver and platinum at the bottom of the series, or as compounds called minerals. A mineral from which a metal can be profitably extracted is an ore, and the unwanted earthly impurities mixed with ore form the gangue. The extraction route depends on where the metal sits in the reactivity series. Highly reactive metals like Na, K, Ca, Mg and Al, which form very stable oxides and cannot be reduced by carbon, are extracted by electrolytic reduction of their molten chlorides or oxides, e.g. molten NaCl gives Na at cathode and Cl2 at anode. Moderately reactive metals like Zn, Fe, Pb and Cu occur as sulphides or carbonates and are first converted to oxides by roasting or calcination, then reduced by carbon. Least reactive metals like Hg occur as sulphides and are obtained by heating alone, as with cinnabar 2HgS + 3O2 -> 2HgO + 2SO2 followed by 2HgO -> 2Hg + O2.
points: Mineral: naturally occurring compound of a metal; ore: mineral from which the metal can be extracted profitably.
Gangue: earthly impurities like sand and rock mixed with the ore, removed during concentration.
Highly reactive metals (K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al): extracted by electrolysis of molten compounds; carbon cannot reduce their oxides.
Electrolysis of molten NaCl: Na metal at cathode and Cl2 gas at anode.
Moderately reactive metals (Zn, Fe, Pb, Cu): sulphide or carbonate ores are converted to oxides and then reduced with carbon.
Least reactive metals (Hg, Ag, Au): often found free or extracted by simple heating of their sulphide ores.
Cinnabar extraction: 2HgS + 3O2 -> 2HgO + 2SO2 on heating in air, then 2HgO -> 2Hg + O2 on further heating.

keyTerms.meaning: Mineral from which a metal can be extracted conveniently and profitably.
Unwanted earthly impurities present in the ore.
Free uncombined state of unreactive metals like gold and platinum in nature.
Extraction method for highly reactive metals using electricity on molten compounds.
HgS, the sulphide ore of mercury.

sections.trick: Three zones of extraction: TOP metals need electricity, MIDDLE metals need fire and carbon, BOTTOM metals need just heat or come free. The harder the metal holds oxygen, the stronger the method needed.
sections.examPointer: Choosing the extraction route for a given ore based on reactivity is a classic 3-5 marker; the cinnabar-to-mercury equations are a repeated 2-marker.

sections.heading: Extraction of Medium-Reactivity Metals: Roasting, Calcination and Thermite
sections.para: Metals in the middle of the series occur mainly as sulphide and carbonate ores. The concentrated ore is first converted to the oxide. A sulphide ore is roasted, heated strongly in excess air: 2ZnS + 3O2 -> 2ZnO + 2SO2 for zinc sulphide, or 2Cu2S + 3O2 -> 2Cu2O + 2SO2 for copper. A carbonate ore is calcined, heated strongly in limited air: ZnCO3 -> ZnO + CO2. The metal oxide is then reduced to metal, usually by carbon: ZnO + C -> Zn + CO2. Copper needs a further self-reduction step: 2Cu2O + Cu2S -> 6Cu + SO2. For highly exothermic reductions, aluminium powder is used: the thermite reaction Fe2O3 + 2Al -> Al2O3 + 2Fe releases so much heat that the iron comes out molten, and this molten iron is used to weld cracked machine parts and railway tracks. The final metal is then refined, most commonly by electrolytic refining.
points: Roasting: heating a sulphide ore strongly in excess air; 2ZnS + 3O2 -> 2ZnO + 2SO2, SO2 fumes are released.
Calcination: heating a carbonate ore strongly in limited air; ZnCO3 -> ZnO + CO2.
Reduction of oxide by carbon: ZnO + C -> Zn + CO2; carbon removes the oxygen.
Copper self-reduction: 2Cu2O + Cu2S -> 6Cu + SO2 in the furnace.
Thermite reaction: Fe2O3 + 2Al -> Al2O3 + 2Fe + heat; molten iron is used to weld railway tracks and cracked machine parts.
Exothermic displacement by aluminium also works on MnO2: 3MnO2 + 4Al -> 3Mn + 2Al2O3.
The extracted crude metal is refined, usually by electrolytic refining, to achieve high purity.

keyTerms.meaning: Strong heating of a sulphide ore in excess air to convert it to oxide.
Strong heating of a carbonate ore in limited air to convert it to oxide.
Highly exothermic reduction of Fe2O3 by Al used for welding rails and machine parts.
Removal of oxygen from a metal oxide using carbon, e.g. ZnO + C.

sections.trick: Sulphide roast, carbonate calcine: S goes with AIR, C goes LIMITED. Thermite = Fe2O3 plus Al, the welding flash of the railway.
sections.examPointer: Roasting vs calcination definitions with one equation each is a standing 3-marker; the thermite reaction and its welding use appear regularly as 2 marks.

sections.heading: Refining, Corrosion Prevention and Alloys
sections.para: The metal obtained by any extraction method still contains impurities and is refined, most commonly by electrolytic refining. In the refining of copper, the impure copper block is the anode, a thin strip of pure copper is the cathode, and copper sulphate solution with a little acid is the electrolyte. On passing current, copper from the anode dissolves as Cu2+ ions and pure copper deposits on the cathode, while insoluble impurities settle below the anode as anode mud, which may contain precious metals like gold and silver. Corrosion of the refined metal is then prevented by painting, oiling, greasing, galvanisation, chrome plating, anodising or alloying. Galvanisation, coating steel with zinc, is used for water pipes and coolers; even if the zinc layer is scratched, zinc corrodes first and protects the iron because zinc is more reactive. Finally, pure metals are often too soft, so alloys are made: steel with carbon, stainless steel with chromium and nickel, brass Cu-Zn, bronze Cu-Sn, solder Pb-Sn and amalgam with mercury.
points: Electrolytic refining: impure metal is the anode, pure metal the cathode, and a solution of the metal salt the electrolyte.
In copper refining, Cu from the anode dissolves as Cu2+ and deposits on the cathode; soluble impurities enter solution and insoluble impurities settle as anode mud.
Corrosion prevention: painting, oiling, greasing, galvanisation, chrome plating, anodising and making alloys.
Galvanisation is coating of iron or steel with zinc; zinc protects iron even when scratched because Zn is more reactive and corrodes first.
Alloy: homogeneous mixture of a metal with other metals or non-metals, made to improve hardness, lustre or resistance.
Important alloys: steel Fe + C, stainless steel Fe + Cr + Ni, brass Cu + Zn, bronze Cu + Sn, solder Pb + Sn, amalgam of any metal with Hg.
Solder has a low melting point and is used for welding electrical wires; pure gold is alloyed with copper or silver for ornaments.

keyTerms.meaning: Purification of a metal by depositing it at the cathode from a solution of its salt.
Insoluble impurities settling below the anode during refining, containing valuable metals.
Zinc coating on iron or steel to prevent rusting.
Homogeneous mixture of a metal with other metals or non-metals to improve properties.
An alloy in which one component is mercury.

sections.trick: Refining memory: Anode impure, cathode pure, anode mud treasures. Alloys: Brass Zn, Bronze Sn, Solder Pb plus Sn, Stainless Cr plus Ni.
sections.examPointer: Electrolytic refining of copper with electrode processes is a repeated 3-marker; alloy compositions and why galvanised iron stays safe are standard 2-markers.

mcqs.question: Which of the following metals is liquid at room temperature?
mcqs.explanation: Mercury is the only metal that exists as a liquid at room temperature, which is why it is used in thermometers.

mcqs.question: Which of the following is a lustrous non-metal?
mcqs.explanation: Iodine crystals have a shining lustrous surface, an exception among non-metals.

mcqs.question: Which of the following oxides show both acidic and basic behaviour?
mcqs.explanation: Al2O3 and ZnO react with both acids and bases, so they are amphoteric oxides; Na2O is basic and CO2 is acidic.

mcqs.question: Sodium and potassium are stored under kerosene because
options: They react violently with air and moisture
mcqs.explanation: Na and K catch fire on contact with the oxygen and moisture of air, so kerosene cuts off both and keeps them safe.

mcqs.question: Which metal reacts vigorously with cold water and starts floating while moving on the surface?
mcqs.explanation: 2Na + 2H2O -> 2NaOH + H2; the reaction is so vigorous and exothermic that the hydrogen catches fire and the low-density metal floats and darts about.

mcqs.question: Iron reacts with steam to give hydrogen and
mcqs.explanation: 3Fe + 4H2O -> Fe3O4 + 4H2; the mixed oxide iron(II,III) oxide is formed when red hot iron meets steam.

mcqs.question: Hydrogen gas is generally not evolved when most metals react with nitric acid because
options: HNO3 is a strong oxidising agent that oxidises H2 to water
Metals do not react with acids
mcqs.explanation: HNO3 oxidises the hydrogen produced into water and is itself reduced to oxides of nitrogen; only Mg and Mn in very dilute HNO3 release H2.

mcqs.question: Aqua regia, which can dissolve gold, is a mixture of concentrated hydrochloric acid and concentrated nitric acid in the ratio
mcqs.explanation: Aqua regia is a freshly prepared 3:1 mixture of conc. HCl and conc. HNO3, one of the most corrosive reagents known.

mcqs.question: Which of the following metals can displace zinc from zinc sulphate solution?
mcqs.explanation: Only metals more reactive than zinc can displace it; Mg lies above Zn in the reactivity series, so Mg + ZnSO4 -> MgSO4 + Zn.

mcqs.question: During the formation of magnesium chloride from Mg and Cl2, the number of electrons lost by Mg and gained by each Cl atom respectively are
mcqs.explanation: Mg -> Mg2+ + 2e- and each Cl gains one electron to become Cl-, so two Cl atoms accept the two electrons of one Mg, giving MgCl2.

mcqs.question: Ionic compounds conduct electricity in the molten state because
options: Ions become free to move and carry current
mcqs.explanation: Melting breaks the rigid lattice and frees the cations and anions, which then move towards the electrodes and conduct electricity.

mcqs.question: The thermite reaction is used for
options: Welding railway tracks and cracked machine parts
mcqs.explanation: Fe2O3 + 2Al -> Al2O3 + 2Fe releases enormous heat producing molten iron, which is used to weld rails and repair machine parts.

mcqs.question: Roasting is applied to sulphide ores while calcination is applied to
mcqs.explanation: Calcination heats carbonate ores like ZnCO3 in limited air, ZnCO3 -> ZnO + CO2, while roasting converts sulphide ores in excess air.

mcqs.question: Heating cinnabar in air and further heating of the intermediate product give
mcqs.explanation: 2HgS + 3O2 -> 2HgO + 2SO2 and then 2HgO -> 2Hg + O2, so mercury metal is obtained from its sulphide ore cinnabar by heating alone.

mcqs.question: In the electrolytic refining of copper, pure copper gets deposited at
mcqs.explanation: Impure copper anode dissolves as Cu2+ ions which travel to the cathode and deposit as pure copper; insoluble impurities form anode mud.

mcqs.question: Galvanisation is the process of coating iron with a thin layer of
mcqs.explanation: Galvanisation means coating iron or steel articles, like water pipes and coolers, with zinc to protect them from rusting.

mcqs.question: The alloy of copper and zinc, used for making utensils and decorative articles, is called
mcqs.explanation: Brass is the copper-zinc alloy; bronze is copper-tin, solder is lead-tin and steel is iron-carbon.

mcqs.question: Solder, an alloy of lead and tin, is used for welding electrical wires because it has
mcqs.explanation: Solder melts at a low temperature, so it can be melted and solidified easily to join wires without damaging them.

mcqs.question: Aluminium utensils do not corrode visibly in daily use because
options: A protective layer of Al2O3 forms on the surface
mcqs.explanation: Aluminium reacts with oxygen of air forming a thin firm layer of aluminium oxide which protects the metal underneath from further corrosion.

mcqs.question: Gold ornaments are made from an alloy of gold rather than pure gold because
options: Alloying with copper or silver makes gold harder and durable
mcqs.explanation: Pure gold is very soft; alloying with copper or silver increases hardness and strength, making ornaments last longer.

boardQuestions.question: Give reasons: (a) Sodium is kept immersed in kerosene. (b) Magnesium ribbon is cleaned by rubbing with sand paper before burning in air. (c) Aluminium articles do not corrode easily even though aluminium is a reactive metal.
boardQuestions.answer: 1) (a) Sodium reacts so vigorously with the oxygen and moisture of air that it catches fire; 4Na + O2 -> 2Na2O and 2Na + 2H2O -> 2NaOH + H2 with ignition. Kerosene cuts off contact with air and moisture, so sodium is safely stored under it. 2) (b) Magnesium slowly reacts with air to form a thin layer of magnesium oxide on its surface. This layer prevents the metal from burning easily, so rubbing with sand paper removes the oxide layer and exposes fresh magnesium for the reaction 2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO. 3) (c) Although aluminium is reactive, it quickly forms a thin, firm and non-flaky layer of aluminium oxide, Al2O3, on its surface. This layer acts as a protective shield and prevents further contact of the metal with air and moisture, so aluminium utensils and foils resist corrosion.

boardQuestions.question: Describe the steps involved in the extraction of a metal of medium reactivity from its sulphide ore and its carbonate ore, writing one balanced equation at each step.
boardQuestions.answer: 1) Concentration: the ore is first powdered and the gangue is removed, for example by froth floatation for sulphide ores. 2) For the sulphide ore, roasting is done by heating it strongly in excess air: 2ZnS + 3O2 -> 2ZnO + 2SO2; sulphur dioxide fumes come out and the zinc oxide remains. 3) For the carbonate ore, calcination is done by heating it strongly in limited air: ZnCO3 -> ZnO + CO2. 4) Reduction of the oxide to metal: the oxide is heated with carbon, which removes oxygen as carbon dioxide: ZnO + C -> Zn + CO2. 5) For exothermic reduction of iron oxide, aluminium powder is used in the thermite reaction: Fe2O3 + 2Al -> Al2O3 + 2Fe, whose heat welds railway tracks. 6) Finally the crude metal is purified by electrolytic refining, where the impure metal is the anode, pure metal the cathode and the salt solution the electrolyte. Thus the sequence is: concentration, conversion to oxide by roasting or calcination, reduction to metal, and refining.

boardQuestions.question: Compare ionic and covalent compounds on the basis of melting point, solubility and electrical conductivity, giving one example of each type.
boardQuestions.answer: 1) Melting and boiling points: ionic compounds have high melting and boiling points because strong electrostatic forces bind the ions, e.g. NaCl melts at about 1074 K; covalent compounds have low melting and boiling points because only weak forces hold their molecules, e.g. naphthalene melts at about 353 K. 2) Solubility: ionic compounds are generally soluble in water and insoluble in organic solvents like kerosene; covalent compounds are generally insoluble in water but soluble in organic solvents. 3) Conductivity: ionic compounds conduct electricity in the molten state and in aqueous solution because their ions become free to move, but not as solids; covalent compounds do not conduct electricity in any state because they have no charged particles, with graphite as the famous exception. 4) Examples: NaCl and MgO are ionic; CH4, CCl4 and glucose are covalent. The table of three contrasts with one example each earns full marks.

boardQuestions.question: Metals A, B, C and D were tested. A displaced B from its salt solution, C displaced A from its salt, and D displaced no metal from any salt solution. Arrange the four metals in decreasing order of reactivity and justify each step.
boardQuestions.answer: 1) A displaced B from B's salt solution, so A is more reactive than B. 2) C displaced A from A's salt solution, so C is more reactive than A. 3) D displaced none of the metals, so D is the least reactive of all. 4) Combining the three observations, the decreasing order of reactivity is C > A > B > D. 5) The rule used throughout is that a more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from its compound in solution, and absence of displacement means the added metal is the weaker one. Such reasoning questions are standard 3-markers in CBSE papers.

boardQuestions.question: Draw the steps in the extraction of copper from its sulphide ore and explain the final refining. Include the equations for roasting and reduction.
boardQuestions.answer: 1) Copper occurs mainly as copper glance, Cu2S, a sulphide ore of a metal in the middle of the reactivity series. 2) Concentration: the powdered ore is concentrated by froth floatation, where the sulphide particles float with oil froth and the gangue sinks. 3) Roasting: the concentrated ore is heated strongly in excess air: 2Cu2S + 3O2 -> 2Cu2O + 2SO2, converting part of the sulphide to copper(I) oxide and releasing sulphur dioxide fumes. 4) Reduction: the remaining copper sulphide reduces the oxide in a self-reduction step: 2Cu2O + Cu2S -> 6Cu + SO2, so blister copper is obtained. 5) Electrolytic refining: the impure copper is made the anode, a thin strip of pure copper the cathode, and acidified copper sulphate solution the electrolyte. On passing current, copper dissolves from the anode as Cu2+ and deposits as pure copper on the cathode. 6) Insoluble impurities like gold and silver settle below the anode as anode mud, which itself becomes a source of precious metals. The pure copper collected at the cathode, better than 99 percent pure, is used for electrical wiring.

boardQuestions.question: Name the reaction used for joining railway tracks. Write its balanced equation and explain why the rails get welded. Which property of aluminium makes this possible?
boardQuestions.answer: 1) The thermite reaction is used for welding railway tracks and cracked machine parts. 2) Equation: Fe2O3 + 2Al -> Al2O3 + 2Fe + heat. 3) Aluminium, being more reactive than iron, displaces iron from its oxide and the reaction releases so much heat that the iron formed is in the molten state. 4) The molten iron flows into the gap between the rails and solidifies on cooling, joining them firmly. The high reactivity of aluminium, which lies above iron in the reactivity series, is the property that makes this possible.

boardQuestions.question: What is corrosion? State the conditions required for the rusting of iron, write the equation, and explain two methods of prevention with reasons.
boardQuestions.answer: 1) Corrosion is the slow eating up of the surface of a metal by the action of air, moisture or chemicals present in the surroundings. 2) Rusting of iron requires both air (oxygen) and moisture (water) together; iron kept in dry air or in boiled water free of oxygen does not rust. 3) The brown flaky deposit is hydrated iron(III) oxide, written as Fe2O3.xH2O, formed by 4Fe + 3O2 -> 2Fe2O3 combined with water. 4) Prevention: (a) Painting or oiling and greasing cut off the contact of the metal surface with air and moisture, so no rust forms; (b) Galvanisation, coating the iron with zinc, works even better because zinc does not rust and, being more reactive than iron, corrodes first to protect the iron underneath. 5) Chrome plating, anodising and making stainless steel are other accepted methods.

boardQuestions.question: Explain the electrolytic refining of copper with a labelled description: name the electrodes, the electrolyte, the reactions at each electrode and the fate of the impurities.
boardQuestions.answer: 1) The impure copper block is made the anode and a thin strip of pure copper is the cathode; the electrolyte is a solution of copper sulphate with a little dilute sulphuric acid. 2) On passing electric current, copper from the impure anode dissolves into the solution as Cu2+ ions: Cu -> Cu2+ + 2e-. 3) These ions move to the cathode and get deposited as pure copper: Cu2+ + 2e- -> Cu, so the cathode gains in mass with almost pure copper. 4) Soluble impurities like iron remain in the solution, while insoluble impurities like gold and silver fall below the anode as anode mud, which is itself commercially valuable. 5) Thus the anode gradually dissolves away and the cathode thickens with refined copper, giving metal of more than 99 percent purity used in electrical wires.

boardQuestions.question: What is an alloy? Write the composition and one use each of brass, bronze, solder and stainless steel, and state why alloys are prepared from pure metals.
boardQuestions.answer: 1) An alloy is a homogeneous mixture of a metal with other metals or non-metals, prepared mainly to improve hardness, strength, lustre and resistance to corrosion. 2) Brass is copper plus zinc, used for utensils and decorative articles. 3) Bronze is copper plus tin, used for statues, medals and bells because it is hard and resists corrosion. 4) Solder is lead plus tin, with a low melting point, used for welding electrical wires together. 5) Stainless steel is iron with chromium and nickel, used for utensils and surgical instruments because it does not rust. 6) Pure metals are often too soft or corrode easily; alloying with suitable elements gives the required hardness, durability and resistance, and also lowers the melting point where needed, as in solder.

boardQuestions.question: Read the source and answer: Four metals P, Q, R and S were added to solutions of their sulphates. P + QSO4 gave PSO4 and Q; R + QSO4 gave RSO4 and Q; but S + QSO4 showed no change. Also, P displaced hydrogen from dilute HCl but S did not. (a) Arrange P, Q, R and S in decreasing reactivity. (b) Which metals lie above hydrogen? (c) Predict what happens when R is added to dilute HCl.
boardQuestions.answer: 1) (a) P displaced Q, so P > Q. R displaced Q, and since Q is the common displaced metal, we know R > Q; the series to be quoted must place R and P both above Q. With the usual interpretation of such questions, R and P both beat Q, and S displaces nothing. 2) Using the given displacement chain, the decreasing order is R > P > Q > S, where R sits at the top because it displaces Q as readily as P does and is taken as the more reactive of the two in the standard version of this problem. 3) (b) P displaced hydrogen from dilute HCl, and R and P are more reactive than Q, which is above hydrogen; hence P, R and Q all lie above hydrogen in the reactivity series, while S, which displaces nothing, lies below hydrogen, like copper or silver. 4) (c) Since R lies above hydrogen, when R is added to dilute hydrochloric acid, it will displace hydrogen vigorously, R + 2HCl -> RCl2 + H2, with brisk effervescence and the gas burning with a pop sound. 5) The key rules: displacement shows the displayer is more reactive, no displacement shows the reverse, and reaction with dilute acids separates metals above and below hydrogen.
